correctness.rationale: The claim is reduced to a finite exact polyhedral optimization. The unit sphere is represented by eight support functionals, active-facet cells are exhausted, linear objectives attain maxima at enumerated endpoints, and every candidate is checked against all support inequalities in \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\). The exact maximum is \(2\sqrt2-1\), and an explicit feasible pair attains it. The proof makes no inference from sampling or timeout.

originality.rationale: The inspected defining and follow-up papers establish the invariant, aliases and general identities but do not state the exact regular-octagon value. The closest inspected regular-octagon paper computes different James--Schäffer constants, and the closest public regular-polygon result treats norm-equilateral perimeter rather than centered triples. Exact-alias, exact-radical, modulus-of-convexity and implication searches did not locate a statement implying \(Y_J(X_8)=2\sqrt2-1\). The inaccessible full text of the 2024 \(J_1\) paper is retained as a residual risk rather than treated as negative evidence.
residual_risks: The full text of Martini--Papini--Wu (2024) was not accessible in the inspected sources; an unlocated exact \(J_1\) example or consequence there remains possible.
Older modulus-of-convexity tables could conceivably encode the same value under different notation; targeted alias and exact-radical searches did not locate one.

value.rationale: \(Y_J\) is a literature-motivated geometric invariant tied exactly to \(\delta_X(1)\). The regular octagonal plane is a canonical benchmark in Banach-space geometry, so an exact value supplies a reusable calibration point for centered-triangle and convexity estimates. The slice is natural rather than an arbitrary parameter choice, and the result resolves the full exact optimization for this norm.
